week.t: NASA: Voyager 1 passed one light-day from Earth on Wednesday evening Singapore time; since 14 Nov it has sent only a bare carrier signal
SpaceX’s CRS-35 Dragon undocked from the station at 1:05 am Singapore time with frozen tumour organoids and a bioprinted blood vessel aboard; splashdown Sunday morning
NASA: Perseverance has paused science while both its UHF radios are checked; one of Mars Odyssey’s reaction wheels stopped and it spent 4–6 Nov in safe mode
NASA Earth Observatory: Cyclone Xavier peaked at 220 km/h near the Cook Islands, the strongest November cyclone east of the date line on record
PIB / DST: a mud core from a wetland in Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve records 2,700 years of the Indian monsoon
NTU: five Year 4 students’ MealGuard spoon, which steadies hand tremors with a servo, wins the University Category of the Engineering Innovation Challenge 2026

tiles.cap: Voyager 1 is now a full light-day away. And since 14 November it has gone quiet
tiles.nums: one light-day: the distance light covers in 24 hours, reached by Voyager 1 at 6:16 pm Singapore time on Wednesday 18 November
tiles.p1: At 6:16 pm Singapore time on Wednesday 18 November, Voyager 1 reached one light-day from Earth, what NASA calls “yet another historic feat”: about 25.9 billion km, or 16.1 billion miles. A radio signal takes a full day to reach it, so NASA’s Voyager team only heard from the probe early on Thursday, about 24 hours after the moment itself. The probe launched in 1977, has been flying for more than 49 years, and left the Sun’s bubble for interstellar space in 2012.
tiles.p2: The twist in NASA’s Thursday release: since 14 November the spacecraft has sent only a bare carrier signal, no science or engineering data. Engineers can hear it; they just cannot read it.
deep: What a light-day means

Light covers about 186,000 miles every second. It reaches the Moon in 1.3 seconds and Neptune in about 4 hours. Voyager 1 is about 20 hours of light beyond Neptune. Send a command today and the earliest possible answer arrives two days later.
How fast, how old

Voyager 1 moves at about 38,000 mph, which is 61,155 km/h. Its power comes from a nuclear generator that loses about 4 watts a year, so engineers have switched three devices to lower-power alternatives to keep the instruments running until at least the 50th launch anniversaries next summer.
The silence

On 14 November a Deep Space Network antenna in Canberra locked on and found a carrier wave but no data. The carrier proves the pointing computer and the transmitter work, so the fault is probably in the computer that packages the data. A similar problem in 2023 is guiding the fix; NASA says the diagnosis may take weeks or longer.
In their words

Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL: “We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly.” Joe Westlake, director of NASA’s Heliophysics Division: “Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler.”
tiles.src: NASA / JPL, NASA’s Voyager 1 Makes History Reaching One Light-Day From Earth, 19 Nov 2026 · NASA Voyager blog, 18 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: Perseverance’s radio missed 25 heartbeats, so the rover switched it off itself
tiles.nums: about how long 25 missed heartbeat pings took before the rover’s fault protection shut the radio down
tiles.p1: On 30 October the main UHF radio on NASA’s Perseverance rover stopped sending its regular heartbeat ping to the rover’s main computer. After 25 missed pings, about 100 seconds, the rover’s fault protection switched the radio off, moved to the backup radio and went into safe mode. Then engineers found the backup was transmitting at about half its expected power. Both radios are off limits until one is judged safe, so science is paused.
tiles.p2: Why it matters: the UHF radios are the links that send big batches of data up to the orbiters. Perseverance is talking straight to Earth through its X-band high-gain antenna instead, which is much slower, so new images are on hold. NASA hopes to resume science by the end of November.
deep: The heartbeat rule

Steven Lee, the project manager at JPL: “Every time it hears the ping, it resets a counter.” When the counter runs too long, the rover assumes the radio is in trouble and protects itself. The rover is stable and communicating with the team.
Odyssey’s wheel

Days later NASA’s Mars Odyssey orbiter sat in safe mode from 4 to 6 November after one of its four reaction wheels stopped. Spacecraft steer by spinning these wheels; another failed in 2013, and at least three are needed. Without them Odyssey points itself with hydrazine thrusters, with fuel for one to two months of that. In a test the stalled wheel did move.
Ten times its design

Odyssey launched in April 2001 and reached Mars in October 2001. It was designed for just over 2.5 years and has now lasted 25, the longest Mars mission ever. It made the first global maps of what Mars is made of and relayed data for Phoenix, Spirit, Opportunity and Curiosity. NASA wants it back at work in the last week of November.
tiles.src: NASA Science, Mars blog, NASA’s Perseverance, Odyssey Teams Investigate Technical Issues, 19 Nov 2026 (updated 20 Nov)
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA/JPL-Caltech (Viking Orbiter 1 mosaic of Mars)

tiles.cap: The Dragon left the station at 1:05 am today. Splashdown off California at dawn tomorrow
tiles.nums: more than 6,300 pounds, about 2,860 kg, of cargo the CRS-35 Dragon carried up on 15 October
tiles.p1: After weather off California scrubbed Wednesday’s attempt, SpaceX’s uncrewed CRS-35 Dragon undocked from the space-facing port of the station’s Harmony module at 12:05 pm US Eastern on Friday 20 November, 1:05 am on Saturday in Singapore, on a command from SpaceX in Hawthorne, California. It then fires its thrusters to move away and is to splash down off California at about 4:55 pm Eastern on Saturday, which is 5:55 am Sunday here. NASA will not stream the splashdown; the result goes on its station blog.
tiles.p2: Why the wait: the undocking planned for Wednesday 18 November was called off for poor conditions at the California splashdown sites, and Thursday was the next opportunity before Friday worked.
deep: What is riding home

A 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct for research on vascular ageing and heart disease; frozen tumour organoids treated in orbit for cancer research; frozen microbial samples from a test of antibiotic-resistant bacteria in space; and a lighting system tested for supporting astronauts’ sleep, after more than three years aboard. The 19 November station blog adds a spacesuit.
The trip up
Dragon arrived on 15 October, two days after launching on a Falcon 9 from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral, carrying more than 6,300 pounds of cargo.
The next truck

Northrop Grumman’s CRS-25 Cygnus XL is set to launch on a Falcon 9 from the same pad no earlier than 10:47 am Eastern on Sunday 29 November, 11:47 pm Singapore time, with about 11,000 pounds of cargo. Astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney are to catch it with the Canadarm2 at 2:35 am Eastern on Tuesday 1 December, 3:35 pm here.
tiles.src: NASA station blog, Dragon Undocks from Station Packed With Science and Cargo, 20 Nov 2026 · NASA advisory M26-087 · NASA, CRS-25 coverage advisory, 18 Nov 2026
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA (Dragon approaching the station, 15 Oct 2026)

tiles.cap: A search that needed 600 years of computer time now takes 10 hours, via code-breaker maths
tiles.nums: spins per second of PSR J1622−7204, a rapidly spinning neutron star, found in 15 years of public Fermi gamma-ray data
tiles.p1: A pulsar is a rapidly spinning neutron star that sweeps beams of radiation toward Earth, like a lighthouse. Finding one in gamma-ray data means guessing its spin rate, its position and how its spin slows, all at once, with millions of trials in each direction. An international team recast that search as a famous puzzle from cryptography, finding the shortest vector in a high-dimensional lattice, and found PSR J1622−7204, spinning 261 times a second, in about 10 hours on a standard processor. The older method had failed on the same object despite about 600 years of processor time.
tiles.p2: Why it works: Dotan Gazith and Barak Zackay of the Weizmann Institute borrowed the lattice trick used in code-breaking and satellite navigation. Gazith: “We have nothing to do with cryptography in our analysis here.” The paper is in Physical Review Letters.
deep: Four dimensions of guessing

Lead author Daniel Pook-Kolb of the Max Planck Institute for Gravitational Physics: “We have a four-dimensional grid, and we must search each direction with millions of trials in it.” The new method is roughly a million times faster than the old one.
Open data

Fermi launched in 2008 and scans the whole sky every three hours; its catalogue has grown from a few hundred sources to thousands. All of its data is public. Elizabeth Hays, Fermi project scientist at NASA Goddard: “Any search that one team is doing, another team can just go and do that and check the search.”
Next
Pulsars with a companion star are even harder to find. The team thinks tens or maybe even hundreds hide in the Fermi data and plans to hunt them with Einstein@Home, the volunteer computing project.
tiles.src: NASA Science, Open Science, NASA Science Data Powers New Method to Discover Hard-to-Find Pulsars, 19 Nov 2026 (Amanda Moon Adams)
tiles.credit: Artist’s impression of Fermi: NASA Goddard / Chris Smith (USRA/GESTAR)

tiles.cap: 220 km/h near the Cook Islands: the strongest November cyclone east of the date line yet
tiles.nums: peak winds of Tropical Cyclone Xavier on Tuesday 17 November, Category 5 on the regional scale
tiles.p1: The Fiji Meteorological Service began tracking a slow-moving disturbance northeast of Samoa and the Cook Islands on Saturday 15 November. Over 29 °C water and with little wind shear it intensified rapidly. NASA’s Aqua satellite caught it at 02:53 UTC on 17 November, 10:53 am Singapore time, with winds of about 195 km/h; later that day they peaked at 220 km/h, Category 5 on the regional scale and Category 4 on the Saffir-Simpson scale. It damaged homes and cut power in the northern Cook Islands, then weakened in dry air and stronger wind shear.
tiles.p2: Why it is unusual: Colorado State University’s Phil Klotzbach calls Xavier the strongest November tropical cyclone east of the International Date Line on record. Storms forming east of the date line fit this year’s El Niño pattern.
deep: The fuel

The Earth Observatory’s story names two ingredients: sea surface temperatures of 29 °C, bath-warm, and low wind shear, little change in the wind between low and high altitude, which let Xavier intensify rapidly.
The season ahead

Xavier is the second named storm of the Southwest Pacific season, after Wati in October. The Fiji Meteorological Service expects 11 to 15 named cyclones this season, with the greatest risk east of the date line; activity usually peaks in February.
Who took the picture
The MODIS instrument on NASA’s Aqua satellite imaged a compact storm with spiralling white cloud bands over blue ocean. NASA Earth Observatory image by Lauren Dauphin; story by Adam Voiland.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, The Stormy Southwest Pacific, 20 Nov 2026
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin, MODIS on Aqua

tiles.cap: One of the driest places on Earth turned purple, and Landsat saw it from orbit
tiles.nums: the number of Atacama blooms counted between 1981 and 2015 in one 2019 paper; this year’s may be the most extensive flowering of the satellite era
tiles.p1: Chile’s Atacama is one of the driest places on Earth. From mid-July 2026 a string of atmospheric-river storms brought one of the heaviest July rain events in decades, and in August back-to-back storms even dropped snow on parts of the desert. Dormant seeds woke up. Landsat 8 imaged the hills about 30 km southwest of Copiapó on 14 September and Landsat 9 again on 24 October: hillsides streaked red-purple, most likely Cistanthe longiscapa, with green patches; a second site about 50 km southwest showed white Nolana baccata flowers in September.
tiles.p2: Why now: a strengthening El Niño weakened the subtropical Pacific high and pushed the Southern Hemisphere storm track toward the equator, so storms that normally pass to the south reached the desert.
deep: Biggest yet?

Plant geographer Andres Moreira-Muñoz of the Pontificia Universidad Católica de Valparaíso says the 2026 bloom appears to be “the most significant to date—in terms of its extent, intensity, and duration,” at least since remote sensing began.
Two sites, two colours

About 30 km southwest of Copiapó the red-purple Cistanthe dominated. About 50 km southwest, white Nolana blooms in September gave way to Cistanthe in October. Ground photos were taken on 24 September and 24 October.
A rare event

A 2014 paper used Landsat to map flowering near Copiapó, and a 2019 paper identified 13 blooms between 1981 and 2015. The Earth Observatory images are by Michala Garrison, using Landsat data from the US Geological Survey.
tiles.src: NASA Earth Observatory, El Niño Rains Paint the Atacama, 19 Nov 2026 (Kathryn Hansen)
tiles.credit: Photo: NASA Earth Observatory / Michala Garrison, Landsat 9 (USGS)

tiles.cap: One tube of mud from a tiger reserve holds 2,700 years of the Indian monsoon
tiles.nums: around 1,100 to 1,200 mm of rain a year or more, which the dense Sal forest of 2,700 to 2,300 years ago implies for central India
tiles.p1: Scientists at the Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences in Lucknow took a sediment core from the Chakradhara Wetland inside Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve in Madhya Pradesh. They sliced it, radiocarbon-dated the layers and identified the pollen grains trapped in each slice. Between 2,700 and 2,300 years ago a strong monsoon supported dense moist forest dominated by Sal (Shorea robusta), which needs about 1,100 to 1,200 mm of rain a year or more. From 820 to 400 years ago the monsoon weakened: moist forest shrank, dry deciduous plants spread, and cereal pollen increased, a sign of farming.
tiles.p2: Why now: the result was published in Quaternary Research and released by PIB on Friday 20 November. Over the last 400 years a strengthening monsoon let the moist forest recover, which the team reads as evidence that tropical forests can regenerate when the climate favours them.
deep: How pollen keeps time

The team divided the core into segments, radiocarbon-dated them and identified the pollen in each. Which plants dominate a layer tells what forest grew: Sal forest implies around 1,100 to 1,200 mm of rain a year or more.
Checking against models

The team, Dr Anjali Trivedi, Anupam Nag and Prof. M. G. Thakkar, compared the pollen record with Earth System Palaeoclimate Simulation models covering the past three millennia. The reserve sits in India’s Core Monsoon Zone, where PIB says high-resolution climate records of the last few thousand years are scarce.
Where exactly

Chakradhara Wetland lies inside Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve in Umaria district, in the north-east of Madhya Pradesh. The Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences is an autonomous institute of the Department of Science and Technology.
tiles.src: PIB / Department of Science and Technology, Pollen from wetland of Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve, 20 Nov 2026 · Quaternary Research, doi 10.1017/qua.2026.10093
tiles.credit: Image: BSIP via PIB (elevation model of Bandhavgarh Tiger Reserve)

tiles.cap: Peel two strips of tape off a table and they push apart. Feynman says why that matters
tiles.nums: if two people at arm’s length each had 1% more electrons than protons, Feynman says the push between them could lift the whole Earth
tiles.p1: The Exploratorium’s Electroscope: press two 10 cm strips of Scotch Magic Tape onto a table, leaving one end hanging over the edge as a handle, peel them off quickly and hang one from each of two straws stuck in clay-filled cups. Bring them face to face from about 15 cm. They swing apart. Now make a sandwich of two strips, sticky on smooth, rip them apart fast and hang them: these two attract. Peeling is a tug-of-war for electrons; two strips peeled the same way end up with the same charge and repel, while the sandwich leaves one strip with extra electrons and the other short of them.
tiles.p2: Why Feynman cares: in Volume II of his lectures he works out that if you and a friend stood at arm’s length and each had just 1% more electrons than protons, the repulsion would be enough to lift a weight equal to the entire Earth. Matter is balanced to better than one part in 10^25, which is why you never notice.
deep: Tell plus from minus

Run a plastic comb through your hair and bring it near each strip. A combed comb carries extra electrons. The strip it pushes away is negative; the strip it pulls toward it is positive or neutral. Then bring your hand near: a neutral hand attracts a charged strip, because the charge shifts electrons inside your skin. The charge leaks away after a few minutes.
How big are these forces?

Feynman, Volume I: the electrical repulsion between two electrons is 4.17 × 10^42 times their gravitational attraction. Two grains of sand a millimetre across, 30 metres apart, would pull with a force of three million tons if their charges did not cancel.
If the tape will not charge
Some table tops do not work. Stick a strip to cardboard, lay a second strip over it and peel the top one off instead. The Exploratorium says not to substitute other brands the first time.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks, Electroscope · The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. II Ch. 1 and Vol. I Ch. 2 and 7

tiles.cap: CERN is lending particle detectors to schools in ten countries. India is one of them
tiles.nums: young people aged 10 to 18 that the first cycle of CERN’s TIMEPIX@school programme is meant to reach, through 50 schools and 120 teachers
tiles.p1: A Timepix chip is a pixel detector born in CERN’s Medipix2 Collaboration: it lets young people visualise and investigate radiation that would otherwise be invisible. On 16 November CERN named the first ten hubs of its TIMEPIX@school programme, one each in Brazil, France, Germany, Greece, India, Italy, Portugal, Slovenia, Spain and the UK, picked from 108 applications from 31 countries. Each hub borrows kits for free, gets online training and works with partner schools for ages 10 to 18.
tiles.p2: Why it is a big deal: the first cycle is meant to reach 50 schools, 120 teachers and 4,000 young people, with a target of more than 20,000 by 2030 and particular emphasis on female pupils and schools in communities under-served and under-represented in STEM.
deep: What you would see

CERN says the kits let young people visualise and investigate radiation that would otherwise be invisible, using pixel detectors originally developed for CERN experiments; related detector technology is used from high-energy physics and medicine to aerospace and art.
Who pays

The programme is backed by the CERN & Society Foundation, which is looking for more donors to grow it. CERN’s teacher programmes already host about 1,000 teachers a year, and its Beamline for Schools competition reaches about 4,500 high-school pupils a year.
Hub, not a shop
Hubs can be schools, universities, institutes or research centres. CERN’s announcement gives no detail yet on which Indian institution hosts the hub.
tiles.src: CERN, TIMEPIX@school programme announcement (Rita Pinho), 16 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: A full Windows PC hiding inside a 670 g keyboard. Plug in a screen and it is a desktop
tiles.nums: the thickness of HP’s EliteBoard G1a, a complete computer measuring 358 × 119 × 18 mm and weighing about 670 g
tiles.p1: HP’s EliteBoard G1a is a full-size keyboard with a number pad that is secretly a whole computer: an AMD Ryzen AI processor (Ryzen AI 5 330, AI 5 340 or AI 7 PRO 350) with a neural unit rated at up to 50 TOPS, 16 GB of DDR5-5600 memory in two slots you can upgrade to 32 GB, a 512 GB NVMe drive you can swap for up to 2 TB, Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6.0. Two USB-C ports carry power and video, one at 40 Gbps and one at 10 Gbps. Plug it into any monitor and it is a desktop. There is no touchpad; HP ships a wireless mouse.
tiles.p2: Why TIME picked it: a computer you carry like a keyboard, for people who hop between desks, weighing less than two pounds. The optional built-in battery is 32 Wh, which HP says is not meant for all-day use away from the mains.
deep: What the tester measured

Tony Polanco of Tom’s Guide ran a Ryzen 7 PRO 350 unit with 32 GB. Geekbench scored 2,793 single-core and 11,424 multi-core; copying 25 GB of files took 16.8 s; converting a 4K video to 1080p took 5 min 41 s; the 3DMark Night Raid score was 20,336 against about 30,000 for comparable laptops; the battery lasted 2 h 26 min driving a portable monitor.
What they found wrong

Polanco: “a steep ask for something so niche,” the membrane key switches are “a bummer,” and “this isn’t a gaming machine.” Anthony Spadafora, also of Tom’s Guide, said the number pad “feels like wasted space” and that the membrane keyboard was “the real deal-breaker” for him. The US price starts at $1,549.
The engineering inside

The case is at least 90% recycled steel and the fan is rated at 38 dB or less. The keyboard deck, memory, drive, battery and speakers are tool-free replaceable; HP says a repair takes under ten minutes. The keyboard is spill-resistant.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Martin Cizmar) · HP, EliteBoard G1a product page · Tom’s Guide, Tony Polanco (updated 7 May 2026) and Anthony Spadafora (12 Jan 2026)

tiles.cap: A 77-inch TV about 1 cm thick, hung like a poster, fed by a wireless box 10 m away
tiles.nums: the depth of LG’s 77-inch OLED evo AI W6 panel, which weighs 20.2 kg without a stand
tiles.p1: LG’s W6 is an OLED television 9.95 mm deep, 1,713 mm wide and 988 mm tall, that hangs flat on a wall with no signal cables running to it. The HDMI signals go into a separate Zero Connect Box (LG’s sheet lists four HDMI inputs that take 4K at 120 Hz, Ethernet, USB and two antenna sockets) that can sit up to 10 m away and sends the picture wirelessly at 4K resolution and up to 165 Hz. The panel runs at 120 Hz natively and up to 165 Hz with variable refresh rate, with a response time under 0.1 ms.
tiles.p2: Why TIME picked it: LG’s original Wallpaper TV, the W7 of 2017, was too thin to hold the hardware that makes a TV smart, so it needed a separate box wired to it, which buyers hid in their walls. The W6 is 4 mm thicker to fit the hardware that talks to the wireless box, and the box can go across the room.
deep: The engineering inside

LG’s Singapore specification sheet lists a 3,840 × 2,160 OLED panel, a peak brightness LG rates at 3.9 times a conventional OLED (its own measurement on a 3% window of the screen), 4.2-channel 60 W speakers, and a Zero Connect Box with four HDMI inputs that it says sends visually lossless 4K at up to 165 Hz over the air.
What reviewers found wrong

Nick Pino of Tom’s Guide, who saw it at CES, notes that every brightness figure so far is LG’s own; his estimate of about 2,340 nits on a 10% window is a calculation, not a measurement. On the price, $5,499 for the 77-inch and $7,499 for the 83-inch, he writes that “it’s not exactly cheap by any stretch of the imagination,” and that “you don’t have to pay such a steep premium just for Hyper Radiant Color technology,” a similar version of which LG’s cheaper C6 and G6 have.
A number to test
Measure your own phone’s thickness with a ruler and compare it with 9.95 mm. Then stand the ruler against the family TV and measure its depth, and picture a 77-inch screen that thin.
tiles.src: TIME Best Inventions 2026 (Justin Pot) · LG Singapore, OLED77W6PSA specifications · Tom’s Guide, Nick Pino, 5 Jan and 22 Apr 2026

tiles.cap: A spoon with a motion sensor and a servo that moves against your hand’s tremor
tiles.nums: university teams beaten by five NTU Year 4 students at the Engineering Innovation Challenge 2026, first prize S$5,000
tiles.p1: MealGuard is a spoon packed with sensors, built by five Year 4 NTU students. A motion sensor detects hand tremors and a servo motor moves the spoon the opposite way so the spoon stays steady. A colour sensor reads a saliva test strip to track glucose. Sound and force sensors notice coughing during a meal and compute a “cough-to-feed ratio”. Everything runs on one microcontroller and streams to a phone app for the user and their carers. On 17 November NTU reported it had been named Champion of the University Category at the Engineering Innovation Challenge 2026, run by the Institution of Engineers, Singapore for National Engineers Day.
tiles.p2: Why they built it: team lead Lee JiaTian Jessica says MealGuard “was inspired by our own family members who experience hand tremors and difficulties eating independently.”
deep: Who did what

Jessica, from Mechanical Engineering, led the tremor control. Chow Ven Yan built the app; Eileen Fun and Tee Jie Xi did the sound and force sensing; Yap Xin Rou did the colour and glucose sensing. The last four are from the School of Chemistry, Chemical Engineering and Biotechnology. Their mentor was Professor Domenico Campolo, co-director of the R3 Institute Singapore.
Breadboard to 3D print
The team built the electronics on a breadboard first, then designed a housing in CAD and 3D-printed it. Ven Yan’s advice: “Think big, trust the process, and never give up.”
Three jobs, one chip

NTU lists three functions in one spoon: tremor cancelling, glucose trend tracking from a saliva strip, and cough detection during meals, all handled by a single microcontroller that streams to the companion app.
tiles.src: NTU School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, NTU students develop smart spoon for safer, more independent meals, 17 Nov 2026

tiles.cap: After a 7.7 quake, NTU flew a mini drone through damaged schools to check their condition
tiles.nums: the magnitude of the earthquake off Flores island, Indonesia, in August 2026
tiles.p1: In August 2026 a magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck off Flores island in East Nusa Tenggara, Indonesia. In November Assistant Professor Fu Yuguang and Dr Yu Xuewen of NTU’s School of Civil and Environmental Engineering went there with Institut Teknologi Bandung and Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency to test two devices in real post-disaster conditions. At RSUD Aeramo, a hospital being rebuilt, they installed two LiftNode units, low-cost Internet-of-Things sensing boxes that process data on the spot, to watch for aftershocks continuously and remotely.
tiles.p2: The drone: SmartBee, a miniature drone for confined spaces, flew indoors through several local high schools and an office building to explore its potential for assessing building condition after an earthquake.
deep: Why a hospital, schools and offices

NTU calls the hospital, schools and government offices critical infrastructure, assessed to establish their condition and safety. NTU says the deployment tested the devices where resources may be limited and operating conditions unpredictable.
Edge intelligence

NTU describes the LiftNode units as low-cost, edge-intelligent Internet of Things sensing platforms: the box itself does the processing for continuous remote aftershock monitoring. Two students, Cui Shuaiwen and Wen Jiaru, supported the team remotely.
Shake tables

In the same week NTU reported that a team from the same school placed fifth and won three awards at IDEERS 2026 in Taipei, where models are shaken on a shake table with simulated earthquake ground motions; theirs used a two-directional base isolation system and a tree-inspired 3D-printed façade.
tiles.src: NTU School of Civil and Environmental Engineering, NTU CEE Researchers Conduct Field Deployment in Flores, Indonesia, 15 Nov 2026 · NTU CEE, IDEERS 2026, 18 Nov 2026
tiles.credit: Photo: NTU Singapore / CEE (field visit to RSUD Aeramo, Flores)

tiles.cap: Stand a mirror between your hands and your brain will believe the wrong one
tiles.nums: hands, one seen and one hidden; your brain merges them into one
tiles.p1: Stand a flat mirror upright on a table so it faces to one side. Put your right hand in front of the reflective side and your left hand behind the mirror, hidden. Look only at the reflection, which looks exactly like your left hand. Snap the fingers of both hands together, then stop one hand. Ask someone to drop a small object into the hidden hand while you watch the reflection.
tiles.p2: What happens: your brain takes the reflected hand for the hidden one. Your nerves say the hidden hand is moving, or has just caught something, while your eyes say the hand you are watching is still. The mismatch feels strange, and that is the point.
deep: Why it works

When you move a hand your brain expects to see it move, and nerve signals from that hand confirm it. The mirror shows a hand that stays still, and the clash between nerves and eyes is what feels so strange.
Where it is used
The Exploratorium notes that mirror therapy, built on this illusion, helps some amputees with phantom-limb pain and some stroke patients regain movement.
Variations
Move only the hidden hand while the seen hand stays still. Try other hand movements while watching the reflection. Hold the mirror by handles instead of standing it on the table.
tiles.src: Exploratorium Science Snacks, Mirrorly a Window

tiles.cap: Every word you say starts in a patch of brain above your left ear, a quarter second early
tiles.nums: about how long before a word is spoken that the left posterior superior temporal gyrus fires
tiles.p1: In 1874 Carl Wernicke described a region of the left temporal lobe needed to understand speech. Some people with damage there also had trouble producing words, and for 150 years nobody could say why a hearing area should matter for talking. Edward Chang’s team at the University of California, San Francisco recorded brain activity in 28 people during surgery for epilepsy or tumours. The region fired while they listened, and fired again about a quarter of a second before they spoke each word. Stimulating only that spot just before speaking disrupted the words.
tiles.p2: Chang: “Every word that you have said today began in that small part above your left ear about a quarter of a second before you said it.” The results were presented on Sunday 15 November at the Society for Neuroscience meeting and published in Science on 19 November.
deep: Cat versus caterpillar
Cells there preferred certain kinds of words. Matthew Leonard of UCSF: “It’s more active when you’re about to say the word caterpillar than when you’re about to say the word cat.”
Reading intentions

Implants in two paralysed volunteers picked up both what they heard and what they intended to say, which points toward speech-restoring devices that read a single region. Jeffrey Binder of the Medical College of Wisconsin: the work “provides convincing evidence that this brain spot is critical for speech production.”
Find it on yourself

Put a finger just above your left ear. The region is under the skull there, in the back part of the upper temporal lobe. Say a long word and a short one and remember the signal left before you heard yourself.
tiles.src: Science News, Laura Sanders, 19 Nov 2026 · A. Silva et al., Science, 19 Nov 2026, doi 10.1126/science.aef8963

tiles.p1: Behavioural scientist Benjamin Lira Luttges at the University of Pennsylvania put it in six words. Do not hand over the things you enjoy and that give you meaning, he says, and decide which skills you want to protect. Trent Cash, a behavioural scientist at the University of Waterloo, adds the mechanism: if we offload a specific skill to AI, we are probably not going to retain that skill particularly well.
tiles.p2: Why it is not scary: Cash also says humans are resilient, and he does not think AI is going to suddenly turn our brains to mush.
deep: The doctors who forgot
Doctors used an AI tool for three months to spot growths during colonoscopies. Back on their own, they did not detect the growths as well.
The readers who gave up

People who used an AI tool to solve SAT questions were more likely to skip questions once the help was removed. The researchers called that particularly concerning, because persistence is key for learning.
